overview: Parasite life cycles only make sense once you know which host gets the adult, sexually mature stage — and which just carries the parasite along.
genZNote: Where the parasite grows up vs where it just passes through.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: The host in which a parasite reaches sexual maturity and, if applicable, undergoes sexual reproduction.
aspects.valueB: The host in which a parasite exists in a larval or asexual stage, required for the parasite to complete its development before infecting the definitive host.

aspects.label: Parasite Stage Carried
aspects.valueA: Adult, sexually mature stage (e.g. adult tapeworm, or the sexual stage of Plasmodium).
aspects.valueB: Larval or asexual stage (e.g. cysticercus larva, or the asexual schizont stages of Plasmodium).

aspects.label: Type of Reproduction Occurring
aspects.valueA: Sexual reproduction of the parasite occurs here (when the life cycle includes a sexual stage).
aspects.valueB: Asexual multiplication typically occurs here, without sexual reproduction of the parasite.

aspects.label: Classic Example — Malaria
aspects.valueA: The Anopheles mosquito, where the sexual cycle (sporogony) occurs.
aspects.valueB: The human, where the asexual cycle (schizogony) occurs.

aspects.label: Classic Example — Taenia
aspects.valueA: The human, harboring the adult tapeworm in the intestine.
aspects.valueB: The pig or cow, harboring the larval cysticercus stage in muscle tissue.

aspects.label: Public Health Implication
aspects.valueA: Controlling the definitive host or interrupting transmission from it can break the cycle at its reproductive source.
aspects.valueB: Controlling the intermediate host (e.g. vector control, meat inspection) is often the more practical prevention strategy.

overlay.commonMisconception: For malaria, humans are the intermediate host and the mosquito is the definitive host — the opposite of what most people assume at first.
